Both regions’ tariffs allow for additional benefit metrics to be included through stakeholder processes such as the Organization of the MISO States in MISO and NYPSC in the NYISO. The flexibility to include alternative benefit metrics allows each region to be responsive, as benefits may change over time and new tools and methods are developed to quantify benefits that were previously difficult to evaluate. In MISO, the evaluation of benefits for individual cost allocation zones allows it to transparently communicate the costs and benefits of a given transmission portfolio to member states and show that MISO’s load-ratio approach yields cost allocations that are roughly commensurate with received benefits. This information can be used by state regulators, policymakers, and other stakeholders when deciding whether to support a given portfolio. In the NYISO, the board is empowered to choose public policy transmission solutions based on qualitative as well as quantitative criteria defined by the NYPSC, such as maximizing the use of existing right-of-way. This holistic approach to selection criteria can support project selection that reflects the complexity of the underlying public policy need and goal. For example, the selected solutions for the AC Transmission Needs project were higher cost than some alternatives but provided greater benefits such as infrastructure resilience and operational flexibility that were deemed important by the NYPSC. By contrast, the ISO-NE tariff does not provide a specific mechanism to evaluate or communicate monetized project benefits. As a result, highly beneficial projects may not be selected because there is no defined means to evaluate whether the additional benefits to the region could outweigh additional cost. Quantifying project benefits is useful for evaluating projects and communicating impacts, but quantified benefits are difficult to use for cost allocation. In general, it is easier to calculate estimated project costs over the multidecade lifetime of a transmission project than the estimated benefits (Shu and Mays 2025). Current tools are designed to quantify a narrow set of benefits, and those benefits can change over the lifetime of the facility (FERC 2024a). The most successful application of benefit evaluation in our case studies was for the purposes of project selection and communication with stakeholders, not cost allocation. 3. Stakeholder engagement and strong champions can increase confidence and support for the project. These groups can build external support for transmission projects among stakeholders; directly inform planning through scenario design, initial studies, and analysis; and provide input on evaluation criteria and cost allocation. In two case studies, stakeholders outside of the RTO/ISO or project developer team initiated the transmission planning process that ultimately led to regional projects. The most influential project champions tend to be state-related stakeholders. In MISO, the governors from Midwest states led efforts to develop more transmission to meet their state needs.
